html:
Ibn Battuta, a traveller from Morocco, reached Delhi in 1334 and served its sultan, Muhammad bin Tughluq, as a judge for about eight years. The Delhi Sultanate then ruled most of India. Ibn Battuta lived on the sultan's gifts and in fear of his temper. He dictated this account in Morocco about twenty years later.

On the next day we arrived at the city of Dihlí [Delhi], the metropolis of India, a vast and magnificent city, uniting beauty with strength. It is surrounded by a wall that has no equal in the world, and is the largest city in India, nay rather the largest city in the entire Muslim Orient.
This king is of all men the fondest of making gifts and of shedding blood. His gate is never without some poor man enriched or some living man executed, and stories are current amongst the people of his generosity and courage and of his cruelty and violence towards criminals. For all that, he is of all men the most humble and the readiest to show equity and justice.
In spite of all we have said of his humility, justice, compassion for the needy, and extraordinary generosity, the sultan was far too ready to shed blood. … Every day hundreds of people, chained, pinioned, and fettered, are brought to his hall, and those who are for execution are executed, those for torture tortured, and those for beating beaten.

In 1342 the sultan sent him as envoy to China, and he did not come back to Delhi.
